analysis:
Both changed files are newly added Swift test files (AutopilotDownloadTests.swift, AutopilotModelSetTests.swift) under provider-swift/Tests. They contain no production code, so they add no runtime attack surface, change no keys, wire protocol, attestation or cache storage, and alter no threat-model controls. Unit 6bb90d8a66da2fa6:0 is metadata-only for the added file; its content is in :1.

The tests exercise security-relevant behavior that lives in unchanged or unseen production code, so they only document its intended contract: (1) the Autopilot effective model set is the persisted selection plus cached builds, capped at 256 IDs, with reportable-ID validation of bounded visible ASCII; (2) downloads require recorded consent and are refused when paused; (3) the closed refusal vocabulary is covered; (4) download disk guards fail closed (reserve, free-space nil, overflow) and the ledger is written with 0600 permissions; (5) a failed self-test refuses only the bytes that failed; (6) a download that completes after consent is revoked joins nothing; (7) a downloaded build is verified against catalog or aggregate hash, or recorded ledger hash, before joining the set, and is never advertised or loaded without an Autopilot operation; (8) re-registration happens only when nothing is busy.

The test fixtures write fake weights to temp directories. I found no secrets, network calls to real endpoints, or insecure defaults. The tests use a dummy coordinator URL of 127.0.0.1:9.

Residual questions for integration: the production implementations (AutopilotDownloadPrefetcher, AutopilotDownloadLedger, ProviderLoop autopilot extensions, AutopilotModelSet) were not in this batch. These tests do not prove those controls correct, e.g. weight-hash verification against the catalog, which relates to T-012 and T-027. The downloads-on-by-default behavior (test lines 123-144) is a product policy that relates to T-016 disk exhaustion, and its safeguards depend on the unseen production code. No threat IDs are invalidated by this PR.
